title: Are patent legal fees deductible as R&D expenses?
description: Patent attorney and USPTO fees are research expenditures deductible under IRC §174A from 2025, but never qualified research expenses for the §41 credit.
summary: Under U.S. federal tax law, attorneys' and USPTO fees a business pays to make and perfect its own patent application are research or experimental expenditures, currently deductible for domestic work under IRC §174A from 2025 onward (amortized under §174 for 2022–2024 and for foreign work), but they are never qualified research expenses for the §41 R&D tax credit.

body.text: Under U.S. federal tax law, attorneys' and USPTO fees a business pays to make and perfect its own patent application are research or experimental expenditures, currently deductible for domestic work under IRC §174A from 2025 onward (amortized under §174 for 2022–2024 and for foreign work), but they are never qualified research expenses for the §41 R&D tax credit.
Jurisdiction: United States federal income tax. Law stated as in force on November 11, 2026. It is general information, not tax or legal advice.
1. Short Answer

Yes, with conditions. Under U.S. federal income tax law, the attorneys' fees for preparing and prosecuting ("making and perfecting") a patent application are explicitly classified as research or experimental (R&E) expenditures under Treasury Regulation §1.174-2(a)(1). That classification makes them deductible or amortizable under the federal R&E cost-recovery rules—specifically Internal Revenue Code (IRC) §174 and, for domestic expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, IRC §174A. They are not, however, qualified research expenses (QREs) eligible for the research tax credit under IRC §41. Legal fees for defending or enforcing a patent in infringement litigation fall under a separate statutory regime outside of §174 and §174A. Recent federal appellate decisions—to which the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) formally acquiesced in October 2026—hold that, at least in Hatch-Waxman Abbreviated New Drug Application (ANDA) patent infringement cases, litigation defense fees are currently deductible ordinary and necessary business expenses under IRC §162(a) and do not have to be capitalized under IRC §263(a).

How a deductible patent perfection fee is recovered depends on the taxable year in which the expenditure is paid or incurred and on whether the underlying research and experimental activity is conducted domestically or outside the United States:

cells: Beginning before Jan. 1, 2022
Former IRC §174
Could be deducted currently under §174(a) or amortized over at least 60 months under §174(b)
Could be deducted currently under §174(a) or amortized over at least 60 months under §174(b)
Beginning after Dec. 31, 2021 and before Jan. 1, 2025
IRC §174 as amended by TCJA §13206
Capitalized; amortized ratably over 5 years (60 months) from the midpoint of the tax year (unless retroactive small business election under OBBBA applies)
Capitalized; amortized ratably over 15 years (180 months) from the midpoint of the tax year
Beginning after Dec. 31, 2024
IRC §174A (added by Pub. L. 119-21) for domestic / IRC §174 for foreign
Deducted currently under §174A(a) (or, by election under §174A(c), capitalized and amortized over at least 60 months)
Still capitalized under §174(a); amortized ratably over 15 years (180 months) from the midpoint of the tax year

body.text: 2. Patent Perfection Fees Are R&E Expenditures
2.1 The regulatory basis

Treasury Regulation §1.174-2(a)(1) states that the term research or experimental expenditures, as used in IRC §174, means expenditures incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business which represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense. The regulation explicitly establishes that the term "includes the costs of obtaining a patent, such as attorneys' fees expended in making and perfecting a patent application." Statutory government filing, examination, and issue fees paid to the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) as part of obtaining the patent fall under the same regulatory category of patent-obtaining costs. The same regulation describes R&E costs as generally including all costs incident to the development or improvement of a product, where a "product" is defined under Treasury Regulation §1.174-2(a)(3) to include any pilot model, process, formula, invention, technique, patent, or similar property used by the taxpayer in its trade or business or held for sale, lease, or license.

One critical regulatory boundary limits this treatment. Under Treasury Regulation §1.174-2(a)(6)(vi), R&E expenditures do not include the costs of acquiring another person's patent, model, production, or process. Consequently, legal fees incurred for negotiating, performing due diligence on, or drafting agreements to purchase or license a patent that someone else developed do not qualify as R&E expenditures under §174 or §174A. Those acquisition-related legal costs are governed by the general intangible capitalization rules of IRC §263(a) and Treasury Regulation §1.263(a)-4 (and, if acquired as part of a trade or business, amortized over 15 years as a §197 intangible). Only the legal and filing costs of obtaining a patent on the taxpayer's own research and development qualify under Treasury Regulation §1.174-2(a)(1).
2.2 The TCJA amortization period (2022–2024)

Section 13206(a) of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA, Pub. L. 115-97) amended IRC §174 for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. For those taxable years, specified research or experimental (SRE) expenditures—which explicitly continued to encompass patent perfection fees under Treasury Regulation §1.174-2(a)(1)—had to be charged to a capital account rather than deducted currently. They were then amortized ratably over a 5-year period (60 months) for domestic research or a 15-year period (180 months) for foreign research, beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year in which such expenditures were paid or incurred.

In IRS Notice 2023-63 (§3.06), the Treasury Department and the IRS clarified that for a full 12-month taxable year, the midpoint is the first day of the seventh month of the taxable year. For a calendar-year taxpayer, therefore, only 6 of the 60 months (10%) of a domestic patent-perfection expenditure could be amortized and deducted in the first taxable year, followed by 20% (12 months) in Years 2 through 5, and the remaining 10% (6 months) in Year 6. Notice 2023-63 (§4.03(1)) and its examples (§4.05, Example 1) also expressly confirmed that patent costs—including attorneys' fees incurred in making and perfecting a patent application and the direct support services of an internal legal department preparing patent applications for a new product—constitute SRE expenditures subject to §174.
2.3 The OBBBA and new §174A (2025 onward)

Public Law 119-21 (139 Stat. 72), commonly called the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), was enacted on July 4, 2025. Section 70302 of the Act added IRC §174A to the Internal Revenue Code. Under §174A(a), notwithstanding IRC §263, there is allowed as a deduction any domestic research or experimental expenditures which are paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year, applicable to amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Section 174A(b) defines "domestic research or experimental expenditures" as research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred by the taxpayer in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business other than expenditures which are attributable to foreign research (within the meaning of IRC §41(d)(4)(F)).

Furthermore, IRC §174A(c) permits a taxpayer to elect to charge domestic research or experimental expenditures to a capital account and amortize them ratably over a period of not less than 60 months, beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits from such expenditures. Because the substantive definition of research or experimental expenditures under Treasury Regulation §1.174-2(a)(1) applies to §174A, domestic patent perfection fees paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, can once again be deducted currently in the year incurred.

Statutory Clarification on "Permanent" Restoration: Secondary commentary frequently describes §174A as a "permanent" restoration of immediate R&D expensing. While Public Law 119-21 enacted IRC §174A without a statutory sunset date or expiration provision (in contrast to certain temporary tax provisions in the Act), "permanent" is a descriptive characterization rather than statutory text; §174A is codification of current law with no stated expiration.
2.4 Foreign patent work stays on 15-year amortization

IRC §174, as amended by Public Law 119-21 §70302, is now titled "Amortization of foreign research and experimental expenditures" and governs exclusively foreign research or experimental expenditures. Under amended §174(a), no current deduction is allowed for foreign R&E expenditures; instead, the taxpayer must charge such expenditures to a capital account and is allowed an amortization deduction ratably over the 15-year period (180 months) beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year in which such expenditures are paid or incurred.

In addition, under IRC §174(d) as amended by OBBBA §70302, if any property with respect to which foreign research or experimental expenditures are paid or incurred is disposed of, retired, or abandoned during the 15-year amortization period, no deduction is allowed on account of such disposition, retirement, or abandonment, and no reduction is allowed to the amount realized upon disposition. Instead, such amortization deduction must continue with respect to such expenditures over the remainder of the 15-year schedule. Revenue Procedure 2025-28 (§2.03(2)) confirms that this stricter version of §174(d) prohibiting basis offset against amount realized applies to property disposed of, retired, or abandoned after May 12, 2025.

Legal Analysis of Sourcing Patent Legal Services: Neither the text of IRC §174 and §174A nor Revenue Procedure 2025-28 contains a specific rule isolating how to source outside patent-prosecution legal services (for example, when a U.S.-based patent attorney drafts an application for a foreign-developed invention, or when foreign legal associates handle national-phase patent filings in foreign patent offices for a U.S.-developed invention). However, IRS Notice 2023-63 (§3.04) states that taxpayers must look to where the SRE activities are performed to determine whether the corresponding SRE expenditures are attributable to foreign research (defined under §41(d)(4)(F) as any research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any territory or other possession of the United States). Moreover, Notice 2023-63 (§4.02(4) and §4.05, Example 1) classifies legal department patent-application preparation as a "direct support" SRE activity. While secondary commentary asserts that the domestic versus foreign classification of patent legal fees turns strictly on where the legal or research labor is physically performed, Treasury and the IRS have not yet issued final regulations specifically addressing whether patent prosecution fees are sourced by the physical location of the legal practitioner performing the drafting or by the location of the underlying experimental research activity to which the patent relates.
3. Transition Rules That Affect 2022–2024 Patent Fees
3.1 Retroactive election for small businesses

Section 3 of Revenue Procedure 2025-28 (2025-38 I.R.B.) implements the retroactive small business election enacted under OBBBA §70302(f)(1). Under this provision, an eligible "small business taxpayer" may elect to apply the amendments made by OBBBA §70302 (including immediate deduction under IRC §174A) retroactively to domestic R&E expenditures paid or incurred in "applicable taxable years," defined as taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025.
To qualify as an eligible small business taxpayer under OBBBA §70302(f)(1)(B) and Revenue Procedure 2025-28 (§3.02), the taxpayer must:

items: Not be a tax shelter as defined in IRC §448(d)(3); and

Meet the gross receipts test of IRC §448(c) for its first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024. Under §448(c), a taxpayer meets the gross receipts test if its average annual gross receipts for the three-taxable-year period ending with the taxable year that precedes such first taxable year does not exceed $25,000,000, as adjusted for inflation. For a taxable year beginning in 2025, that inflation-adjusted threshold is $31,000,000 (per Revenue Procedure 2024-40 and Revenue Procedure 2025-28).

body.text: Domestic patent perfection fees that were capitalized and amortized in 2022, 2023, or 2024 under TCJA §174 are eligible to be deducted retroactively under this small business election because they constitute domestic R&E expenditures.

Procedural Clarification: Simplified summaries often state that small businesses claim this relief merely by filing amended returns. In fact, Revenue Procedure 2025-28 establishes detailed procedural mechanisms: an eligible small business taxpayer may make the election by filing an amended federal income tax return, an administrative adjustment request (AAR) under IRC §6227 (for BBA partnerships), or—for certain 2024 returns where Revenue Procedure 2025-28 granted an automatic six-month extension—a superseding return, or via an automatic accounting method change under modified Section 7.01 of Revenue Procedure 2025-23, accompanied by a mandatory statement titled "FILED PURSUANT TO SECTION 3.03 OF REV. PROC. 2025-28." Furthermore, under OBBBA §70302(f)(1)(C), the election must be made on or before July 6, 2026 (one year after the July 4, 2025 date of enactment, adjusted for the weekend under IRC §7503) or before the expiration of the period of limitations for credit or refund under IRC §6511, whichever is earlier.
3.2 Recovering unamortized amounts for all other taxpayers

Statutory Precision on Unamortized Balance Acceleration: For any taxpayer that does not qualify for (or chooses not to make) the small business retroactive election, OBBBA §70302(f)(2)(A) and Revenue Procedure 2025-28 (modifying Section 7.02 of Revenue Procedure 2025-23) provide an election to accelerate the recovery of remaining unamortized domestic SRE amounts that were paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025. Specifically, the taxpayer may elect to deduct any remaining unamortized domestic R&E balance (including unamortized domestic patent-prosecution fees):

items: In full in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (e.g., 100% deducted on the 2025 return for a calendar-year taxpayer); or
Ratably over the 2-taxable-year period beginning with the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (e.g., 50% in 2025 and 50% in 2026 for a calendar-year taxpayer).

body.text: This acceleration is implemented as an automatic change in method of accounting under IRC §§446 and 481 (with a modified §481(a) spread or cut-off mechanic as specified in Revenue Procedure 2025-28) filed on Form 3115 (or short-form statement where permitted for the 2025 year). A taxpayer that makes neither election simply continues amortizing its 2022–2024 capitalized domestic balances over the remainder of their original 60-month TCJA schedule while deducting newly incurred 2025 domestic R&E currently under IRC §174A.
3.3 Hypothetical example

Hypothetical. Assume a calendar-year C corporation that is not an eligible small business taxpayer (because its average annual gross receipts exceed $31,000,000) paid $100,000 of domestic patent-prosecution attorneys' fees in 2023 to prepare and file patent applications on its internally developed technology:

items: 2023 TCJA Amortization: Under TCJA §174, the $100,000 expenditure is capitalized and amortized over 60 months ($100,000 ÷ 60 months = $1,666.67 per month). Because amortization begins at the midpoint of the 2023 calendar year (July 1, 2023), the corporation deducts 6 months × $1,666.67 = $10,000 on its 2023 return.
2024 TCJA Amortization: On its 2024 return, the corporation deducts a full 12 months × $1,666.67 = $20,000.
Unamortized Balance at January 1, 2025: Entering the 2025 taxable year, the remaining unamortized capital account balance is $100,000 − $10,000 − $20,000 = $70,000 (representing 42 remaining months).

OBBBA §70302(f)(2) Recovery Options for 2025 Onward: Under OBBBA §70302(f)(2)(A) and Revenue Procedure 2025-28, the corporation may elect to deduct the entire $70,000 unamortized balance in 2025, or it may elect to deduct $35,000 in 2025 and $35,000 in 2026 ($70,000 ÷ 2). If the corporation makes neither election, it continues its original schedule: deducting $20,000 per year in 2025, 2026, and 2027, and the final $10,000 (6 months) in 2028 ($20,000 × 3 + $10,000 = $70,000).

Treatment of New 2025 Patent Fees: If the same corporation pays an additional $100,000 of domestic patent-prosecution fees in 2025, it may deduct the entire $100,000 in 2025 under IRC §174A(a). Conversely, if the 2025 expenditure is attributable to foreign research governed by IRC §174(a), it must be capitalized over 180 months starting at the midpoint of 2025, yielding a 2025 deduction of $100,000 ÷ 180 months × 6 months = $3,333.33.

body.text: 4. Why Patent Legal Fees Are Not Section 41 Credit Expenses
4.1 The statutory tests
Under IRC §41(d)(1), to constitute "qualified research" eligible for the federal Research and Development (R&D) Tax Credit, an activity must satisfy a rigorous four-part statutory test:

items: Section 174A Eligibility Test (§41(d)(1)(A)): The expenditures with respect to such research must be eligible to be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC §174A. (Statutory Note: Prior to the enactment of Public Law 119-21, §41(d)(1)(A) cross-referenced §174; OBBBA §70302(b)(1) amended §41(d)(1)(A) to cross-reference "domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A" for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024).

Technological in Nature Test (§41(d)(1)(B)(i)): The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information which is technological in nature (meaning the process of experimentation must fundamentally rely on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science under Treasury Regulation §1.41-4(a)(4)).

Business Component Test (§41(d)(1)(B)(ii)): The application of that information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer (defined in §41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer).

Process of Experimentation Test (§41(d)(1)(C)): Substantially all (at least 80% under Treasury Regulation §1.41-4(a)(6)) of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a permitted purpose listed in §41(d)(3)(A) (a new or improved function, performance, or reliability or quality).

body.text: Separately, even when an underlying project meets all four tests of §41(d)(1), the R&D tax credit under IRC §41(a) is computed strictly on "qualified research expenses" (QREs) as exhaustively defined in IRC §41(b)(1). Under §41(b)(1) and (2), QREs are restricted to:

items: In-house research expenses: (i) Wages paid or incurred to an employee for "qualified services" performed by such employee (engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research under §41(b)(2)(B)); (ii) amounts paid or incurred for "supplies" used in the conduct of qualified research (tangible property other than land, improvements to land, or depreciable property under §41(b)(2)(C)); and (iii) under §41(b)(2)(A)(iii), amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research; and

Contract research expenses: Generally 65% of any amount paid or incurred by the taxpayer to any person (other than an employee of the taxpayer) for the performance on behalf of the taxpayer of qualified research (§41(b)(3)(A)).

body.text: 4.2 Applying the tests to patent fees

Domestic patent perfection fees pass the first threshold test under IRC §41(d)(1)(A) because Treasury Regulation §1.174-2(a)(1) explicitly designates them as R&E expenditures. However, patent prosecution and legal fees fail to qualify for the IRC §41 credit on both activity-level and cost-category grounds:

First, under the activity tests of IRC §41(d)(1)(B) and (C) and Treasury Regulation §1.41-4(a)(3)–(5), the work performed by patent attorneys and patent agents in conducting prior-art searches, drafting claims, and prosecuting applications before the USPTO is undertaken to resolve legal uncertainty regarding the scope of intellectual property protection and statutory patentability under Title 35 of the U.S. Code—not to resolve technical uncertainty regarding the capability, method, or appropriate engineering design of the business component itself through a scientific process of experimentation.

Second, and equally dispositive, fees paid to outside patent counsel do not fit into any statutory category of QREs under IRC §41(b). Outside legal fees are not employee wages (§41(b)(2)(A)(i)), are not tangible supplies (§41(b)(2)(A)(ii)), and constitute "contract research expenses" under §41(b)(3) only to the extent the outside contractor is paid to perform "qualified research." Because drafting and prosecuting patent claims is a legal service rather than qualified research (and does not qualify as "direct support" of actual laboratory experimentation under Treasury Regulation §1.41-2(c)(3)), outside patent legal fees are categorically excluded from the §41 credit calculation. Similarly, wages of in-house patent attorneys drafting patent applications are excluded from QREs because administrative, legal, and property-protection functions do not constitute engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting the actual conduct of qualified research under §41(b)(2)(B). Including patent legal fees in Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) is a well-documented compliance error that triggers disallowance during IRS examination.
4.3 Credit rates

Statutory Correction on Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) Rates: Secondary industry commentary sometimes states that the federal R&D credit is "typically 6% of QREs for the first three years of claims and 14% under the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) after that." That phrasing misstates the statutory trigger in IRC §41(c)(4). The statute does not link the 6% or 14% rate to how many years a taxpayer has claimed the credit.

Instead, under IRC §41(c)(4)(A), a taxpayer electing the Alternative Simplified Credit calculates a credit equal to 14% of so much of the taxpayer's QREs for the taxable year as exceeds 50% of the average QREs for the 3 taxable years preceding the taxable year for which the credit is being determined. Under the special rule of IRC §41(c)(4)(B)(ii), if the taxpayer has no qualified research expenses in any one of the 3 taxable years preceding the taxable year for which the credit is being determined, the ASC rate is 6% of the QREs for the current taxable year (with no base-amount subtraction). While a startup or newly innovating company with no prior three-year history of QREs will fall under the 6% rule of §41(c)(4)(B)(ii) until it has incurred QREs in each of the three preceding taxable years, the statutory determinant is the presence of QREs in all three prior years—not whether the taxpayer previously filed a claim. In all events, patent legal fees do not enter either the current-year QRE pool or the three-year historical base calculation because they are never QREs.
4.4 Outside patent counsel and the 65% contract research rule

Under IRC §41(b)(3)(A), "contract research expenses" mean 65% of any amount paid or incurred by the taxpayer to any person (other than an employee of the taxpayer) for qualified research. (This percentage rises to 75% for amounts paid to a qualified research consortium under §41(b)(3)(C), and 100% for certain energy research under §41(b)(3)(D)).

Statutory Correction on Amortization vs. Credit Haircut: Some commentary conflates IRC §41(b)(3)(A) with IRC §174, implying that only 65% of third-party contractor or legal payments were required to be capitalized and amortized under the TCJA. That is legally incorrect. The 65% statutory haircut exists solely in IRC §41(b)(3)(A) for purposes of computing the §41 research credit. Under IRC §174 (for 2022–2024 domestic SREs and all foreign SREs) and IRC §174A (for 2025+ domestic R&E), 100% of eligible research or experimental expenditures—including 100% of qualifying patent perfection legal fees paid to third-party law firms—are included in the §174 capital account or §174A deduction base. Conversely, for the §41 credit, 0% of outside patent counsel fees qualify because patent prosecution is not qualified research.
4.5 Coordinating the credit with the §174A deduction (§280C(c))

IRC §280C(c) prevents a taxpayer from receiving an unreduced double tax benefit (both a full deduction/capitalization basis and a full tax credit) on the same dollar of research expenditure. Following the enactment of Public Law 119-21 §70302(b)(2), IRC §280C(c) operates as follows for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024:

items: General Reduction Rule (§280C(c)(1)): The domestic research or experimental expenditures (as defined in IRC §174A(b)) otherwise taken into account as a deduction under §174A(a) or charged to a capital account under §174A(c) must be reduced by the amount of the research credit determined under IRC §41(a).

Election of Reduced Credit (§280C(c)(2)): To avoid reducing its §174A deduction (which often simplifies state tax conformity and accounting), a taxpayer may elect on a timely filed return (including extensions) to claim a reduced §41 credit. Under §280C(c)(2)(B), the reduced credit equals the regular §41(a) credit minus the product of that credit multiplied by the maximum corporate income tax rate under IRC §11(b) (currently 21%, meaning the taxpayer retains 79% of the gross credit and preserves 100% of its §174A deduction). Once made for a taxable year, the election is irrevocable for that year.

body.text: Under Revenue Procedure 2025-28 (§§4 and 5), however, an eligible small business taxpayer that makes the retroactive OBBBA §70302(f)(1) election to apply §174A to its 2022–2024 taxable years is granted special relief to make a late §280C(c)(2) reduced-credit election, or to revoke a previously made §280C(c)(2) election, for those 2022–2024 applicable taxable years.
Statutory Corrections on §280C(c):

items: Subsection Citation: Prior to the TCJA and OBBBA redesignations, the reduced-credit election was located in §280C(c)(3). In the current Internal Revenue Code (as amended by TCJA and OBBBA §70302), the reduced-credit election is codified at IRC §280C(c)(2), while IRC §280C(c)(3) houses the controlled-group allocation rules (incorporating §41(f)).

Inapplicability to Foreign R&E: Commentary stating that §280C(c)(1) reduces amounts capitalized for foreign research expenditures under §174 is inaccurate. Current IRC §280C(c)(1) explicitly applies only to "domestic research or experimental expenditures (as defined in section 174A(b))," and foreign research is statutorily ineligible to generate a §41 credit in the first place under §41(d)(4)(F). Because patent legal fees generate $0 of §41 credit, §280C(c) affects the deduction of patent fees only indirectly to the extent the taxpayer's aggregate §41(a) credit (generated by engineering wages, supplies, and qualified contract research) reduces the taxpayer's overall pool of deductible domestic R&E expenditures under §174A.

body.text: 5. Patent Costs Listed as Excluded in Secondary Literature

Cross-checking those specific exclusion lists reveals that the phrasing regarding "taking out a patent after a successful research project," "pre-project patent searches," and the verbatim bulleted list of general corporate exclusions (such as "tender expenses," "canteens," and "directors' management fees") originates from guidance on Australia's R&D Tax Incentive (Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 (Cth) Div 355), where all expenditure incurred in acquiring or obtaining rights to a patent is statutorily or administratively ineligible. Under United States federal income tax law, each of these items must be evaluated strictly under the Internal Revenue Code and Treasury Regulations:

items: Costs of Obtaining a Patent After Technical Development: Unlike Australian tax law, U.S. Treasury Regulation §1.174-2(a)(1) expressly provides that research or experimental expenditures "includes the costs of obtaining a patent, such as attorneys' fees expended in making and perfecting a patent application." In U.S. patent practice, a non-provisional patent application is routinely drafted, filed, and prosecuted during or immediately after the laboratory development of the invention. Nothing in IRC §174, §174A, or Treasury Regulation §1.174-2 disqualifies patent perfection fees simply because the underlying invention succeeded or is intended for commercial sale; in fact, Treasury Regulation §1.174-2(a)(1) states that "[t]he ultimate success, failure, sale, or use of the product is not relevant to a determination of eligibility under section 174," and §1.174-2(a)(3) defines "product" to include a patent held for sale, lease, or license. Thus, U.S. law includes patent-obtaining legal fees in §174/§174A, while excluding them from the §41 credit.

Pre-Project Patent and Prior-Art Searches: For the IRC §41 credit, a pre-project patentability or freedom-to-operate legal search is ineligible because it is a legal evaluation rather than technological experimentation under §41(d)(1) and does not fall within §41(b) QRE categories. Under IRC §174/§174A, whether a pre-project prior-art search conducted by an attorney qualifies depends on whether it is incurred as part of "making and perfecting a patent application" or is directly "incident to the development or improvement of a product" under Treasury Regulation §1.174-2(a)(1), as opposed to a general commercial or market-feasibility investigation excluded under §1.174-2(a)(6) (such as management studies or market research).

Marketing Trademarks and Commercialization Costs: Under U.S. law, Treasury Regulation §1.174-2(a)(6)(v) explicitly excludes expenditures for "advertising or promotions" from §174 R&E treatment, and IRC §41(d)(4)(D)(iii) excludes advertising or promotions from the §41 credit. Furthermore, trademark registration and branding legal fees are not "costs of obtaining a patent" under §1.174-2(a)(1); instead, trademark acquisition costs are capitalized under IRC §263(a) and Treasury Regulation §1.263(a)-4.

Acquired Patents: Treasury Regulation §1.174-2(a)(6)(vi) explicitly excludes "[t]he acquisition of another's patent, model, production or process" from §174/§174A, and such costs are likewise excluded from §41 QREs.

Routine Post-Issuance Patent Maintenance Fees: Once the USPTO issues a utility patent, the patentee must pay periodic statutory maintenance fees at 3.5, 7.5, and 11.5 years after grant (35 U.S.C. §41(b)) to keep the patent in force. Because the patent has already been obtained, post-issuance maintenance fees are not costs of "making and perfecting a patent application" under Treasury Regulation §1.174-2(a)(1), nor are they §41 QREs. Instead, recurring post-grant maintenance fees paid to preserve an existing patent used in the taxpayer's trade or business are generally deductible as ordinary and necessary business expenses under IRC §162(a).

General Corporate and Administrative Exclusions under U.S. Law: U.S. law enforces parallel exclusions through Treasury Regulation §1.174-2(a)(6) (excluding quality control testing, efficiency surveys, management studies, consumer surveys, advertising, and promotions), IRS Notice 2023-63 (§4.03(2), which explicitly excludes general and administrative [G&A] service department costs—such as payroll, human resources, accounting, tax preparation, and general finance—that only indirectly benefit research activities, as well as interest on debt used to finance SRE activities), and IRC §41(b) (which restricts QREs strictly to direct research wages, supplies, and qualified contract research).

body.text: 6. Patent Litigation Fees: §162(a) Rather Than §263(a)
6.1 The issue

Legal fees incurred in defending against a patent infringement lawsuit (or prosecuting an infringement claim against a competitor) are not costs of "making and perfecting a patent application" under Treasury Regulation §1.174-2(a)(1) and do not involve experimental laboratory research, so they fall entirely outside IRC §174, §174A, and §41. Instead, the central tax controversy governing patent litigation fees is whether they are immediately deductible as ordinary and necessary business expenses under IRC §162(a) or must be capitalized under IRC §263(a) and Treasury Regulation §1.263(a)-4 as amounts paid to acquire, create, or "facilitate" the acquisition or creation of an intangible asset, or to defend or perfect title to intangible property.

In a major series of cases involving generic pharmaceutical manufacturers, the IRS contended that legal fees incurred by generic drug makers in defending patent infringement lawsuits brought by brand-name drug companies under the Hatch-Waxman Act (35 U.S.C. §271(e)(2)) had to be capitalized under IRC §263(a) and Treasury Regulation §1.263(a)-4(b)(1)(v) because the litigation allegedly "facilitated" the creation or acquisition of an intangible asset—namely, Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval of an Abbreviated New Drug Application (ANDA) containing a Paragraph IV certification.
6.2 Mylan

In Mylan Inc. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, 156 T.C. 137 (2021), aff'd, 76 F.4th 230 (3d Cir. 2023) (Nos. 22-1193, 22-1194, 22-1195, decided July 27, 2023), the taxpayer incurred roughly $130 million in legal fees during the 2012 through 2014 taxable years in connection with Paragraph IV ANDA filings and resulting Hatch-Waxman patent litigation.
In the U.S. Tax Court (156 T.C. 137), the court bifurcated Mylan's legal fees into two distinct categories:

items: Paragraph IV Notice-Letter Costs (Capitalized): Legal fees incurred to prepare and send the statutory Paragraph IV notice letters to brand-name patent holders were required to be capitalized under IRC §263(a) and Treasury Regulation §1.263(a)-4 because sending the notice letter is a mandatory statutory step required to complete the ANDA regulatory approval process, and those capitalized costs were then amortized over 15 years under IRC §197.

Patent Infringement Litigation Defense Costs (Deductible under §162(a)): Legal fees incurred to defend the subsequent Section 271(e)(2) patent infringement lawsuits were held to be currently deductible as ordinary and necessary business expenses under IRC §162(a).

body.text: On appeal of the litigation-cost issue, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit affirmed the Tax Court in Mylan Inc. v. Commissioner, 76 F.4th 230 (3d Cir. 2023). The Third Circuit rejected the Commissioner's expansive interpretation of "facilitate" under Treasury Regulation §1.263(a)-4(e)(1)(i) and held that defending a Hatch-Waxman patent infringement suit is not a required step in obtaining FDA approval of an ANDA (as the FDA can approve an ANDA even while patent litigation remains pending once the 30-month stay expires, and a generic manufacturer can win FDA approval yet lose the patent suit, or vice versa). Instead, the Third Circuit recognized that patent infringement litigation is a normal, ordinary tort-like business dispute arising out of the generic manufacturer's efforts to compete in commerce.

Citation and Holding Corrections: Secondary summaries frequently misattribute the citation 156 T.C. 137 (2021) to the Third Circuit; 156 T.C. 137 (2021) is the decision of the U.S. Tax Court, whereas the Third Circuit's appellate opinion is 76 F.4th 230 (3d Cir. 2023). Additionally, any summary of Mylan must explicitly note that the pre-litigation Paragraph IV notice-letter preparation fees were capitalized, while only the litigation defense fees were held currently deductible under §162(a).
6.3 Actavis

In Actavis Laboratories FL, Inc. v. United States, 131 F.4th 1345 (Fed. Cir. Mar. 21, 2025) (No. 2023-1320), aff'g 161 Fed. Cl. 334 (2022), the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit reached the identical conclusion, affirming the U.S. Court of Federal Claims and holding that a generic drug manufacturer's Hatch-Waxman patent litigation defense expenses are fully deductible as ordinary and necessary business expenses under IRC §162(a) and are not required to be capitalized under IRC §263(a).

Writing for the Federal Circuit, the court applied both the common-law "origin of the claim" test established by the U.S. Supreme Court in Woodward v. Commissioner, 397 U.S. 572 (1970), and the regulatory "facilitate" standard of Treasury Regulation §1.263(a)-4. Under the origin-of-the-claim test, the Federal Circuit held that the origin of a Hatch-Waxman lawsuit is a claim of patent infringement by the brand-name patent holder seeking to protect its market monopoly and block commercial sales—not the acquisition of an intangible FDA license by the generic applicant. Under the regulatory test, aligning with the Third Circuit's decision in Mylan, the Federal Circuit held that defending the patent suit does not facilitate the acquisition or creation of an FDA-approved ANDA.

Factual Precision on Dollar Amounts: In Actavis, the exact Hatch-Waxman litigation expenses at issue as stated in the court opinions were $3,882,951 for the 2008 taxable year and $8,481,237 for the 2009 taxable year (approximately $3.88 million and $8.48 million, rather than the truncated "$3.8 million and $8.4 million" figures cited in some secondary summaries).
6.4 Update: IRS acquiescence in AOD 2026-04

In Action on Decision (AOD) 2026-04 (issued in October 2026), the Internal Revenue Service formally announced its Acquiescence in the decisions of both the Third Circuit in Mylan Inc. v. Commissioner, 76 F.4th 230 (3d Cir. 2023), and the Federal Circuit in Actavis Laboratories FL, Inc. v. United States, 131 F.4th 1345 (Fed. Cir. 2025). AOD 2026-04 specifically addresses the issue of whether legal expenses incurred by a generic drug manufacturer in defending Hatch-Waxman patent infringement suits must be capitalized under IRC §263(a) or are currently deductible under IRC §162(a).

By issuing an Acquiescence in AOD 2026-04, the Office of Chief Counsel announced that the IRS accepts the holdings of the Third and Federal Circuits and will no longer litigate the capitalization of Hatch-Waxman patent infringement defense costs across any judicial circuit. (While an Action on Decision bears a standard administrative legend noting that it is not an affirmative ruling that may be cited as binding legal precedent by taxpayers, it governs IRS examination and litigation posture nationwide).
6.5 Limits of the litigation holdings

Both Mylan and Actavis—as well as earlier foundational precedent such as Urquhart v. Commissioner, 215 F.2d 17 (3d Cir. 1954)—operate within the boundaries of the Supreme Court's origin-of-the-claim doctrine in Woodward v. Commissioner, 397 U.S. 572 (1970), and Treasury Regulation §1.263(a)-4(d)(9)(i). Under those authorities, patent litigation legal fees are not universally deductible in every factual circumstance:

items: Infringement and Damages Litigation (Generally Deductible under §162(a)): Where a patent owner sues an alleged infringer to protect its business operations and recover lost profits or royalties (Urquhart, 215 F.2d at 19–21), or where an accused infringer defends its right to manufacture and sell products in its trade or business against infringement claims (Mylan; Actavis), the litigation expenses are ordinary and necessary business expenses deductible under IRC §162(a)—even when routine invalidity counterclaims are raised as an affirmative defense in the infringement action.

Litigation to Defend or Perfect Title or Acquire a Patent (Capitalized under §263(a)): Conversely, under Treasury Regulation §1.263(a)-4(d)(9)(i) and §1.212-1(k), amounts paid to another party to defend or perfect title to intangible property (such as a lawsuit over ownership, inventorship assignment, or fraudulent conveyance of a patent), or litigation arising directly out of the process of acquiring a patent asset (Woodward, 397 U.S. at 577; Safety Tube Corp. v. Commissioner, 168 F.2d 787 (6th Cir. 1948)), are capital expenditures under IRC §263(a) that must be added to the cost basis of the patent rather than deducted under §162(a). Furthermore, trademark validity or rebranding disputes often face stricter capitalization scrutiny under §263(a) where the dispute involves acquiring or establishing long-term brand rights rather than defending against tortious infringement.

cells: Attorneys' fees & USPTO filing fees for making and perfecting the taxpayer's own patent application

Yes. Domestic: currently deductible from 2025 onward under §174A(a) (or electively amortized over ≥60 months under §174A(c)); capitalized and amortized over 5 years in 2022–2024 under TCJA §174 (subject to OBBBA transition/retroactive relief). Foreign: capitalized and amortized over 15 years under §174(a).
No. Excluded because legal services do not resolve technological uncertainty via experimentation and do not fit §41(b) wage, supply, or qualified contract research categories.
Legal & transaction costs of acquiring another person's patent
No. Expressly excluded from R&E expenditures; capitalized under §263(a) (and amortized over 15 years under §197 if acquired as part of a trade or business).
No. Excluded from §41 QREs.
Patent or trademark legal costs incurred for marketing, branding, or promotions
No. Advertising and promotional expenditures are excluded from R&E; trademark registration costs are not patent-obtaining costs and must be capitalized under §263(a).
No. Advertising and promotions are statutorily excluded from qualified research.
Pre-project patentability or prior-art search legal fees

Fact-dependent under U.S. law. Qualifies under §174/§174A only if incurred in making and perfecting a patent application or directly incident to product development; excluded if part of general commercial/market feasibility studies.
No. Legal prior-art searches do not constitute technological experimentation or §41(b) QREs.
Routine post-issuance USPTO patent maintenance fees (3.5, 7.5, and 11.5 years)
No. Not costs of "making and perfecting" a patent application under §1.174-2(a)(1); generally deductible as ordinary and necessary business expenses under IRC §162(a).
No. Post-grant administrative maintenance of an existing asset is outside §41(b) and §41(d).
Hatch-Waxman (ANDA) & commercial patent infringement litigation defense fees
No (Not §174/§174A costs). Currently deductible in the year incurred as ordinary and necessary business expenses under IRC §162(a); not capitalized under §263(a).
No. Litigation defense is not qualified research under §41.
